name: Updating an Element in the List (Case 1)
description: Construct a program that initializes a list with three values, changes the first element in the list, and finally, prints the list.
code:
#Step 1: Define a list of three integer values
lst = [123, 100, 39]
#Step 2: Update the list element
lst[0] = 2
#Step 3: Print the list
print(lst)

1.content: #Step 1: Define a list of three integer values

commentList: Purpose: This line creates a list with three integer values and stores it in the variable lst so you can update an element later and then print the whole list.
Syntax breakdown: lst is the variable name, = is the assignment operator, and [123, 100, 39] is a list literal — square brackets hold the items and commas separate them.
Semantics: When this line runs Python builds a list object containing the three numbers and makes lst refer to that same object; when you do lst[0] = 2 you change the first element of that same list.

Common errors and misconceptions: If you forget the brackets (for example write lst = 123, 100, 39) you create a tuple instead of a list; missing commas or unmatched brackets cause a syntax error; using quotes around the numbers would make them strings, not integers.

Best practices: Use a clear name (e.g., numbers) instead of vague names when helpful, include spaces after commas for readability (as shown), and remember that lists are mutable — updating elements modifies the existing list rather than creating a new one.
You are replacing the first element of the list named lst with the integer 2 so that the list entry that was 123 becomes 2; this is the core change the problem asks for.
You use lst[0] to select the element at index 0 (Python uses 0-based indexing, so index 0 is the first item) and the = operator to assign the new value 2 to that position.
If lst does not exist you'll get a NameError, and if lst is an empty list or shorter than 1 you'll get an IndexError because there's no element at index 0 to assign to.
If lst refers to a tuple (which is immutable) attempting this assignment raises a TypeError; also avoid accidentally writing lst[0] == 2, which would perform a comparison instead of assignment.
Because lists are mutable, this assignment changes the list in place — any other variable that refers to the same list will see the updated value, so be mindful of shared references.

As a best practice, you can check len(lst) > 0 before assigning if you're not sure the list has enough elements, use a descriptive variable name instead of lst, or use append/insert when you mean to add a new element rather than replace one.
You call print(lst) to display the current contents of the list on the screen; after the earlier update this will show [2, 100, 39].

You are using Python's print function with lst as the argument: Python evaluates lst to the list object, converts that object to a readable string form (the list literal with brackets and commas), and writes it to standard output followed by a newline.

Be careful: if lst were not defined you would get a NameError. In Python 3 you must use parentheses (print(lst)); writing print lst would cause a SyntaxError. Also remember print only shows the value—it does not change the list.

If you want a different format (no brackets, custom separators, or pretty printing), you can format the output (for example print(*lst) to print elements separated by spaces, or use pprint/json for nested structures). For larger programs prefer logging over print for better control.

You might choose this because you think the first item in a list is index 1. Step-by-step: this line is valid Python and assigns the value 2 to the element at index 1. In the given list, that changes the second element, not the first, so the printed list will show the second item replaced while the original first item stays the same. You may pick this if you habitually count items starting from 1. Why this is wrong for the goal: it updates the wrong position (the second element) rather than the element you intended to change. The problem with this line is that it targets a different element in the list, so the program's visible result will be incorrect even though the code runs without error.

Step-by-step: this line performs a comparison between the element at index 0 and the value 2, producing True or False, but it does not assign anything to the list. Because the result of the comparison is not used or stored, the list remains unchanged and the program continues without error. You may select this option thinking it sets a value, but it only checks equality. The impact is that the list will be printed exactly as it started, so the intended change does not happen. The key issue is that this line performs a test instead of updating the list element.

commentList: You might choose this because you know how to add items to a list and assume inserting at position 0 will replace the current first element. Step-by-step: this line inserts the value 2 at the start of the list, shifting all existing elements to the right. The list now has one more element and the old items remain after the new one. You may pick this if you want the value 2 to appear first but aren't aware that insert adds rather than replaces. The effect is that the program will print a longer list with 2 added at the front instead of updating an existing element. The core mistake is using a method that grows the list rather than changing an existing element in place.
